note: Evidence examples (9 -> 18): two per capability, one conceptual and one applied. Draft for review.

capabilities.statement: Map and question the scholarly discourse around a topic

evidence.title: Discourse map tagged with Barnett's domains of critical being
evidence.example: You build a one-page map of the scholarly debate on a topic, grouping authors by the position they take and adding one question to each group. Using Barnett's (1997) idea of critical being across knowledge, self and world, you tag each question as aimed at the claim itself, at who it affects, or at what you had assumed. This shows you can map a discourse and question it, not just list sources (for example, three positions on screen time and early language development in education studies).
evidence.artefact: An annotated one-page discourse map with author groups, a question on each group and a short key explaining the Barnett tags.

evidence.title: Source and stakeholder map for a food bank coordinator
evidence.example: You volunteer with a local food bank and the coordinator wants to know what is being said about food insecurity among students. You map the main voices, such as university reports, a charity briefing and two research articles, note where they agree and disagree, and write down the questions they leave open. This shows you can find who is saying what and question it before anyone acts (for example, asking whether the published figures include part-time and commuting students).
evidence.artefact: A two-page briefing note with a map of sources and positions, signed off by the volunteer coordinator.
grounding: professional: Scans a field, market or policy area to find its key players, positions and open questions before acting.
professional: ESCO thinking skills: acquiring and managing information

genericOutcomes.title: Critical map of positions within a field of debate
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can describe the main positions within a scholarly debate and identify which questions about it remain unresolved.
genericOutcomes.example: You take a topic currently debated within a field and build a map of the main positions people take, noting where they draw on evidence and where they simply assert a view. For each position you write down at least one question that is still open, rather than treating the debate as already settled. This demonstrates mapping a body of discourse and interrogating it rather than only summarising what has been said.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written map of positions, each tagged with an open question still to resolve.
grounding: benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: Questioning the state of a field before acting
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can map the key positions in a field of debate and note the open questions before acting on any of them.
genericOutcomes.example: Before committing to a course of action, you first establish what is already being said within the relevant field: who holds which position, where views converge, and where they conflict. You note the questions that remain unresolved so that any decision you make is built on an accurate picture rather than on one persuasive source. This demonstrates mapping a discourse and questioning it before acting on it.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short note identifying key positions in a field and the questions still open, used to inform a decision.
grounding: professional: Scans a field, market or policy area to find its key players, positions and open questions before acting.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

capabilities.statement: Apply critical thought to the choices made when searching, reading and planning

evidence.title: Search and reading decision log tagged with Delphi dispositions
evidence.example: While preparing a first-year essay, you keep a log of each choice you make: the search terms, the filters, which sources you read and in what order. Beside each choice you note which disposition from Facione's (1990) Delphi report it reflects, such as open-mindedness or diligence in seeking relevant information. This shows critical thought at work before any writing starts (for example, in sport science, choosing to read a study that challenges the textbook view on static stretching).
evidence.artefact: A search and reading decision log of about ten entries, each tagged with a Delphi disposition and a one-line reason.

evidence.title: Planning sheet questioning a manager's brief at a café
evidence.example: In a part-time café job, your manager asks you to find out whether switching to compostable cups is worth it. Before collecting anything, you write down the scope of the question, the sources you will trust, such as council guidance and an independent review, and the assumptions you notice in the brief. This shows you apply critical thought to searching and planning from the start (for example, noting that the most persuasive figures come from the cup supplier itself).
evidence.artefact: A one-page planning sheet listing scope, chosen sources and flagged assumptions, with your manager's written comment on it.
grounding: professional: Questions the sources, scope and assumptions of a piece of work from the start, not only at review.

genericOutcomes.title: Judgement reached through weighing conflicting evidence
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain how weighing the strength and relevance of conflicting evidence leads to a reasoned judgement rather than a quick preference.
genericOutcomes.example: You are given two pieces of evidence that point in different directions and, instead of picking the one you find easiest to believe, you set out the strength and relevance of each, then explain which argument the evidence best supports. You state the judgement you reach and the reasoning that gets you there, so someone else could follow and test it. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments to reach a reasoned judgement.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written judgement setting out the evidence weighed, the reasoning used and the conclusion reached.

genericOutcomes.title: Recommendation after weighing the evidence
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can identify which of two conflicting pieces of evidence better supports a course of action and state the reasoning behind that choice.
genericOutcomes.example: You are asked to recommend a course of action and given information that does not all point the same way. You weigh the strength and relevance of each piece before making your recommendation, state which evidence carries most weight and why, and note what would change your mind. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments critically to reach a judgement someone else can act on.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short recommendation stating the evidence weighed, the judgement reached and what would change it.
grounding: professional: Weighs competing evidence or arguments before recommending a course of action.

capabilities.statement: Treat being critical as a habit of mind, not a switch for assessment

evidence.title: Weekly reflections on everyday questioning using Gibbs' Reflective Cycle
evidence.example: Over four weeks you write short reflections, using Gibbs' (1988) Reflective Cycle, on moments when you questioned something outside assessment: a news story, a claim in a lecture, a statistic in a group chat. The analysis and conclusion stages show you asking why you questioned it and what you would do next time. This shows being critical becoming a habit, not something saved for marked work (for example, a psychology student questioning a viral post about learning styles).
evidence.artefact: Four dated reflective log entries following the six stages of Gibbs' cycle, with a closing paragraph on what has changed.

evidence.title: Questions raised as a student society committee member
evidence.example: As a society committee member, you start questioning the society's own habits: claims in recruitment posts, figures in the treasurer's report, assumptions behind event plans. You raise these questions at ordinary meetings where nothing is being assessed, and you check claims before they are acted on. This shows criticality as a habit of mind in everyday settings (for example, asking where the claim that most members prefer evening events came from, then running a quick poll).
evidence.artefact: Meeting minutes showing the questions you raised, the poll results and a short note on the decisions that changed.

genericOutcomes.title: Habitual evaluation of everyday evidence and claims
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain why evaluating evidence and arguments critically should be a standing habit rather than a response reserved for assessment.
genericOutcomes.example: You adopt a standing habit of evaluating evidence and arguments wherever you meet them, not only when a piece of work is being judged. When you notice a claim, whether in a conversation, a report or a passing comment, you pause to ask what evidence supports it and whether the reasoning holds up before accepting or acting on it. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments critically as an ongoing disposition rather than a switch turned on for assessment.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written account of a claim you queried, the evidence you checked, and the judgement you reached.

genericOutcomes.title: Evaluating claims as routine professional practice
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can routinely question the evidence behind everyday claims and judge whether the reasoning holds up before relying on them.
genericOutcomes.example: In your day-to-day work, you treat evaluating evidence and arguments as a standing habit rather than a step you perform only when a piece of work is being reviewed. Whenever a claim is made, a figure is quoted or a plan is proposed, you ask what evidence backs it and whether the reasoning stands up before you rely on it. This demonstrates reaching reasoned judgements through critical evaluation as an everyday working habit, not an occasional exercise.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A brief record of a claim checked during routine work, the evidence considered, and the judgement reached.
grounding: professional: Treats evaluating evidence and arguments as a standing habit built into everyday work, not reserved for formal review.

capabilities.statement: Recognise the critical thinking skills of analysis and evaluation

evidence.title: Past questions classified by revised Bloom's taxonomy
evidence.example: You collect eight past essay and exam questions from your programme and classify each by the process it demands in Anderson and Krathwohl's (2001) revised Bloom's taxonomy, separating analyse (break down, compare, organise) from evaluate (check, critique, judge). You justify each classification from the steer words and flag questions that need both. This shows you can recognise analysis and evaluation when a task asks for them (for example, in law, 'analyse the reasoning in Donoghue v Stevenson' against 'to what extent was the decision justified').
evidence.artefact: A table of eight questions showing the steer word, the Bloom process, your justification and a tutor's comment on two borderline cases.

evidence.title: Annotated placement requests sorted into analysis or judgement
evidence.example: On an engineering placement you receive three requests from your supervisor. Before starting, you note for each whether it asks for analysis (how a system works and why it fails), a judgement between options, or both, and you confirm your reading with your supervisor. This shows you recognise analysis and evaluation when the brief does not use academic steer words (for example, 'can you look into the pump' turning out to mean 'recommend which replacement to buy').
evidence.artefact: Your annotated copies of the three requests and a short email exchange confirming what each one asked for.
grounding: professional: Recognises when a brief asks for analysis, for a judgement between options, or for both.
professional: Revised Bloom's taxonomy: Analyse, Evaluate

genericOutcomes.title: Judging the rigour of a piece of work
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse a piece of work by distinguishing what was done from how rigorously it was carried out, then evaluate each separately.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a piece of work to review, you first separate the analytical task, working out what was done and how the parts fit together, from the evaluative task, judging how rigorously it was carried out. You examine the method or reasoning behind the work and state how far it holds up, rather than simply describing what the work contains. This demonstrates the critical thinking skills of analysis and evaluation applied to judging rigour.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written judgement on a piece of work, separating the analysis from the evaluation of its rigour.

genericOutcomes.title: Assessing the rigour of a piece of work
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can evaluate the rigour of a piece of work by analysing its method before judging how far its conclusions can be trusted.
genericOutcomes.example: You are asked to check whether a piece of work can be relied on. You analyse how it was carried out, what was measured and how, before judging how rigorous that method actually is and what confidence it supports. You report your judgement separately from your analysis so that others can see how you reached it. This demonstrates critical thinking skills of analysis and evaluation used to judge the rigour of real work.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short report analysing how a piece of work was carried out and judging how rigorous it is.
grounding: professional: Recognises when a brief asks for analysis, for a judgement between options, or for both.

capabilities.statement: Analyse and evaluate a scholarly interpretation

evidence.title: Critique of a historian's interpretation using Delphi core skills
evidence.example: You take one scholarly interpretation and work through it with three core skills from Facione's (1990) Delphi report: analysis, to identify its claims and evidence; evaluation, to judge the strength of its reasoning; and inference, to say what follows and what the author leaves out. You then reach your own view on how far it holds. This shows you can weigh an interpretation, not just summarise it (for example, a historian's argument that the 1834 Poor Law was driven chiefly by cost).
evidence.artefact: A two-page critique sheet mapping the interpretation's argument, your judgement of its strengths and weaknesses, and your inference, with sources cited.

evidence.title: Memo weighing a vendor's wellbeing report against alternatives
evidence.example: On a placement with a school's pastoral team, you are given a supplier's report claiming its wellbeing app reduces pupil anxiety. You analyse its claims, sample and method, then weigh it against two other options the school is considering, and say which is best supported. This shows you can analyse and evaluate an argument made by someone else for a real decision (for example, noting that the report's only study was funded by the supplier and had no comparison group).
evidence.artefact: A one-page memo comparing the report with two alternatives, with your placement supervisor's written feedback.
grounding: professional: Analyses an argument, report or proposal and weighs it against the alternatives.

genericOutcomes.title: Evaluating theory and research with reflection
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can evaluate a theoretical interpretation by analysing the evidence and assumptions it rests on and reflecting on their own standpoint.
genericOutcomes.example: You take a piece of theory or published research and evaluate it critically, examining the evidence it rests on and the assumptions built into it, then reflect on how your own background might shape your reading of it. You reach a judgement on how far the interpretation is supported and note what further evidence would strengthen or weaken it. This demonstrates critically and reflectively evaluating theory and research rather than simply reporting what it claims.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short evaluation of a theory or study, noting assumptions, supporting evidence, and what would strengthen the judgement.

genericOutcomes.title: Reflective evaluation of research behind a proposal
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse the research behind a proposal and evaluate how far the evidence supports it before reaching a justified conclusion.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a proposal that rests on a particular theory or body of research, you evaluate how well the evidence supports it, reflecting on what assumptions the proposal takes for granted and where your own standpoint might affect your judgement. You set out your conclusion and the reasoning behind it so that someone else could check your thinking. This demonstrates critically and reflectively evaluating theory and research when acting on a real proposal.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short evaluation of the research behind a proposal, with your conclusion and the reasoning that supports it.
grounding: professional: Analyses an argument, report or proposal and weighs it against the alternatives.

capabilities.statement: Read a journal article strategically by its structure and method

evidence.title: Reading route record for three articles, method first
evidence.example: You read three journal articles by their structure: abstract and conclusion first, then the method, then the results, and only then the introduction if you need it. For each method section you apply the Delphi skills of interpretation and evaluation (Facione 1990) to decide how far the findings can be trusted. This shows you choose how to read rather than reading front to back (for example, in nursing, checking whether a falls-prevention trial randomised wards or individual patients).
evidence.artefact: A reading record for three articles showing the order you read sections, a method summary and a verdict on how far you rely on each.

evidence.title: Method check of a published study during a software internship
evidence.example: During a summer internship in a software team, you are asked whether a published study supports adopting a new testing tool. You go straight to the method and results, check how the tool was tested and on what kind of code, and only then read the discussion. You brief the team on whether the method justifies the claim (for example, noting that the study used small open-source projects quite unlike your team's large, older system).
evidence.artefact: Your annotated copy of the study with method notes, plus the short written summary or slide you gave the team.
grounding: professional: Reads research and technical reports selectively and checks their method before relying on their findings.

genericOutcomes.title: Verifying findings by reading the method first
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse a study's method ahead of its findings to judge whether the approach actually supports the conclusions drawn.
genericOutcomes.example: Rather than accepting a reported finding at face value, you read the method section of a piece of research before anything else, checking how the evidence was gathered and whether the approach actually supports the conclusion drawn. Only once you trust the method do you read the wider argument and reach your own judgement on the evidence presented. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments critically by reading strategically rather than passively.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short note on a study's method, stating whether the approach actually supports its reported conclusion.

genericOutcomes.title: Checking a study's method before acting on it
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can evaluate whether a published study's method is strong enough to support a decision before relying on its reported findings.
genericOutcomes.example: Before relying on a published study to support a decision, you read its method and results closely, checking how the work was carried out and on what it was tested, then judge whether the approach is strong enough to support the claim. You report your judgement so others can see the reasoning, rather than passing on the headline finding uncritically. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments critically to reach a reasoned judgement.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written judgement on whether a study's method is strong enough to support a decision based on it.
grounding: professional: Reads research and technical reports selectively and checks their method before relying on their findings.

capabilities.statement: Form and justify judgements on the relative importance of factors

evidence.title: Ranked factor judgement built on explicit evaluation criteria
evidence.example: You rank the factors that explain an outcome and justify the order against criteria you state in advance, such as strength of evidence, size of effect and scope. In Anderson and Krathwohl's (2001) terms you work at the level of evaluate, checking and critiquing each factor against those criteria rather than listing them. You also say what evidence would change your ranking (for example, in geography, ranking rainfall, land use and drainage as causes of repeated flooding in one town).
evidence.artefact: A ranked factor table with criteria and weightings, a 300-word justification and a note on what evidence would change the ranking.

evidence.title: Live brief recommendation on which factor to tackle first
evidence.example: On a live brief for a small business, you investigate why repeat customers have fallen, weigh the possible causes, and recommend which one the owner should tackle first, stating why and what you set aside. This shows you can form and justify a judgement someone will act on (for example, for an independent bike shop, judging from complaints and sales data that slow repair turnaround matters more than price).
evidence.artefact: A recommendation report with ranked factors and reasons, and the client's written response on the decision they took.
grounding: professional: Recommends one option over others and states why, so that a decision can be taken on it.

genericOutcomes.title: Reasoned ranking of competing factors
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can justify a ranking of competing factors by weighing the evidence and arguments for each and keeping the reasoning open to challenge.
genericOutcomes.example: Given several factors that could explain an outcome, you weigh the evidence and arguments for each one critically, then rank them by relative importance and justify the order you reach. You state the reasoning behind your ranking clearly enough that someone else could follow it and challenge any step. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments critically to reach a reasoned judgement on which factors matter most.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written ranking of competing factors with reasons, open to challenge at each step.

genericOutcomes.title: Recommending priorities after weighing the factors
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can construct a recommendation that names the most important factor, justifies that priority, and states what evidence would change the judgement.
genericOutcomes.example: Facing several possible explanations for a problem, you weigh the evidence and arguments behind each one and reach a judgement on which factor matters most, stating clearly what led you there. You put this judgement into a recommendation that names what should be addressed first and what evidence would change your mind. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments critically to reach a reasoned judgement that someone else can act on.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short recommendation naming the priority factor, the reasoning behind it, and what would change the judgement.
grounding: professional: Recommends one option over others and states why, so that a decision can be taken on it.

capabilities.statement: Write critically, synthesising sources in the discipline's vocabulary

evidence.title: Essay section redrafted from summary into synthesis
evidence.example: You redraft one section of an essay from source-by-source summary into synthesis, grouping sources by the point they make and using the field's own terms. You annotate the redraft to show where it moves from evaluate to create in Anderson and Krathwohl's (2001) revised taxonomy, putting sources together into a new structure that carries your own position (for example, in design, combining usability and inclusive design studies into an argument about hospital wayfinding signs).
evidence.artefact: Before and after versions of one essay section, annotated to show the synthesis moves, the discipline terms used and your own position.

evidence.title: Policy briefing synthesising evidence for a council team
evidence.example: On a placement with a council's public health team, you write a briefing for councillors that draws together research, local data and national guidance. You lead with your conclusion, organise the evidence by theme rather than by source, and use the terms the team works with. This shows you can write critically for readers who must act (for example, framing a briefing on hot food takeaways near schools in terms of health inequalities and upstream interventions).
evidence.artefact: A two-page policy briefing with an evidence synthesis table and your supervisor's sign-off on its accuracy.
grounding: professional: Writes a recommendation that draws the evidence together and reaches a justified conclusion in the field's own terms.

genericOutcomes.title: Synthesis reaching a reasoned written conclusion
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can synthesise several sources into a single reasoned argument, making explicit how strongly the evidence supports its conclusion.
genericOutcomes.example: You bring together several sources that each make a partial point and combine them into a single piece of writing that reaches its own reasoned conclusion, rather than reporting each source separately. You weigh how strongly each source supports your position and make that reasoning visible in the text itself. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments critically and writing the resulting judgement in a form others can follow.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short piece of writing combining several sources into one argument, with reasoning shown throughout the text.

genericOutcomes.title: Written recommendation synthesising evidence into one conclusion
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can construct a written recommendation that draws evidence from several sources together and justifies a clear conclusion for others to act on.
genericOutcomes.example: You write a recommendation that pulls together evidence from several sources into one coherent argument, rather than presenting each source in isolation, and you reach a justified conclusion that states what should happen next. You make clear how strongly the evidence supports that conclusion and where it is more tentative. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments critically and reaching a reasoned judgement that others can act on.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written recommendation combining evidence from several sources into one justified conclusion, with its reasoning made explicit.
grounding: professional: Writes a recommendation that draws the evidence together and reaches a justified conclusion in the field's own terms.

capabilities.statement: Write with authority, aware of how own stance shapes the argument

evidence.title: Stance analysis and positionality commentary on a dissertation chapter
evidence.example: You analyse a draft dissertation chapter using Hyland's (2005) model of stance, marking hedges, boosters, attitude markers and self-mention. You revise so your stance is visible and deliberate, then write a commentary on how your own position shaped which arguments you made strongest. This shows authority that comes from knowing your stance, not hiding it (for example, a teacher researching behaviour policy noticing they boosted claims that matched their own classroom experience).
evidence.artefact: A colour-coded chapter extract showing stance markers before and after revision, with a 500-word positionality commentary.
grounding: model: Stance and engagement model of academic interaction (Hyland 2005)

evidence.title: Insider research report stating the author's position
evidence.example: In a work-based master's project, you research a practice in your own organisation and write a report for senior leaders. You state your stance as an insider at the start, show where it may have shaped your reading of the evidence, and still make a clear case with authority. This shows you can write as an expert while being open about your position (for example, a charity fundraising manager reviewing the donor strategy they helped design).
evidence.artefact: The final report with its positionality section, plus written feedback from a senior leader or academic supervisor.
grounding: practice: work-based master's project in own organisation

genericOutcomes.title: Writing authoritatively while declaring your own stance
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can critique their own standpoint, explaining how it may have shaped which evidence they judged most persuasive in reaching a conclusion.
genericOutcomes.example: When you reach a judgement on evidence and arguments, you write it up in a way that both states your conclusion with authority and makes visible the stance from which you reached it, rather than presenting your view as if it came from nowhere. You note where your own position might have shaped which evidence you found most persuasive. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments critically while remaining accountable for the standpoint behind the judgement.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short piece of writing that states a conclusion with authority and names the stance it was argued from.
grounding: model: Stance and engagement model of academic interaction (Hyland 2005)

genericOutcomes.title: Owning your stance when reporting a judgement
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can justify a written judgement with authority while disclosing the standpoint it was argued from, so others can assess the reasoning accordingly.
genericOutcomes.example: After weighing evidence and arguments to reach a judgement, you write it up with authority while being explicit about the position you argued from, rather than presenting the conclusion as neutral. You flag where your own stake in the matter might have shaped which evidence carried most weight for you, so readers can judge the argument accordingly. This demonstrates evaluating evidence and arguments critically while remaining transparent about the standpoint behind the reasoned judgement.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written judgement that states its conclusion clearly and discloses the standpoint the reasoning came from.
grounding: professional: States a personal or organisational position at the outset and shows where it may shape the reading of evidence.
